tweets.text: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Excited to announce Projects, which are Perplexity's hubs for agent and human collaboration. Most of my time now lives in Projects, where agents automatically manage their own persistent files and collaborate with native tools. Projects are Perplexity's core for collaboration: as agents become more long-running, they will need more agent-native ways to persist and self-improve: memories, skills, and files. But until today, agents have lacked a central hub for collaboration that allows for a persistent area for knowledge work. That place is Projects, not individual chats or files. Projects come packaged with an set of CLI tools intentionally designed for agents to collaborate across files, projects, and with other agents. Importantly, both individual and project identities are fully functional. Individually-scoped connectors are supported as usual, but so are project-level credentials. A project-level brain agent manages the project and provides objective summaries and memories. Agents do the execution but humans still do the steering with notifications and permissions checks. Internally at Perplexity, the canonical way to work is now to start in Slack (each Project connects with at least one Slack channel), spawn multiple threads of conversation in parallel, accept most first passes, and follow up in Perplexity's apps when refinement is needed. The future of knowledge work is looking bright: work is incredibly efficient with tools like Computer, leaving more time for curiosity and learning. Projects is the next step in the vision that Spaces began for collaboration and persistent storage of context. We're excited to see how you use Projects and we will learn from your feedback to keep pushing the frontier of what is possible when agents and humans work together to build real businesses. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). New newsletter: THE FOUR HORSEMEN OF THE AI BUBBLE APOCALYPSE I am neither anti-AI nor certain that AI is a bubble. But the last four weeks have made clear that the AI buildout now faces a very clear quadruple-headed risk hydra. 1. A spending risk, as the hyperscalers run low on cash and take on $170b in annual debt—which is more than the projected UK deficit. 2. A revenue risk, as open-weight models threaten to compress the margins of frontier labs ... and as AI become the sort of internationally competitive asset-heavy industry requiring stable and determined long-term policy consistency, which is arguably China's competitive advantage. 3. A political risk, as anti-AI populism becomes one of the easiest applause lines, even as AI becomes a more and more foundational pillar of US economic growth 4. A technological risk, as the frontier labs bear down on RSI, which I think could significantly change the basic business model of the labs, as compute costs rise and rise for a set of super-advanced models that are fit for, and affordable to, a small minority of users (in, eg, cyber security) In one sentence: The capabilities of AI are becoming more powerful, while some economic underpinnings of the AI buildout—and, as we’ll discuss, the political support for AI—are becoming more vulnerable. Today's (long, 5k word) piece deeply considers each risk and also—because over-confidence in this space is typically a sign that you're not thinking hard enough—I offer the strongest reason to think each risk might be overblown. derekthompson.org/p/the-four…

Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Most evaluations of agents conducting AI research focus on narrow, verifiable tasks. But AI research is often open ended. Researchers pick hypotheses, decide what evidence is appropriate, and recognize a failing approach. We gave agents research questions from two unpublished papers, six days, and thousands of dollars of API credits and compute. The authors of the original papers then reviewed the AI-generated papers. They unambiguously rejected agents' outputs. arxiv.org/pdf/2607.27191 We call these "shadow evaluations", since the agents are shadowing the original research effort by the authors. Agents were fluent at most *engineering* tasks They conducted serious literature reviews, debugged GPU environments, ran hundreds of experiments, and turned in camera-ready LaTeX without human help. We also found no evidence of reward hacking. If anything, we found the opposite: the agents started with marketable claims and walked them back to negative results as the evidence came in. Neither agent output was close to the bar of a top conference paper Both papers suffered from similar failures: poor judgment about the bar for an AI paper submitted to a top conference, the lack of creative problem solving and ineffective backtracking, poor awareness of resources, and instruction drift. 1) Lack of judgment about the bar for a top conference. The agents had a poor model of the bar for an AI paper submitted to a top conference. We allowed agents to self review their papers. Despite the poor paper quality, their reviews predominantly labeled the papers "weak rejects". 2) Lack of creative problem-solving to address feedback. When they received negative reviews, the agents typically narrowed their hypothesis and claims, rather than working out creative ways to address these concerns. 3) Ineffective backtracking. The agents dropped their most ambitious hypotheses within the first fifteen hours of carrying out the experiment and never changed course afterwards. 4) Poor resource awareness. Both runs ended with over half the API budget unspent. One agent declared itself done seven hours before the deadline, right after its own self-reviewer returned another reject. 5) Instruction drift. They did not follow explicit instructions on minimum exploration time, incorporating feedback for reviews, and on paper length (the outputs exceeded the page limits in both cases). This research design has many limitations Limitations include the small sample size, non-blind reviews, and the reviewers knowing that the work was AI-generated. We also couldn't test Anthropic's strongest model, because Fable 5 is deliberately limited on frontier AI research tasks, so ended up using OpenClaw with Opus 4.8 (extra-high) for our main experiments and Codex with Sol 5.6 (ultra) for a robustness check. But we think the research design is still helpful in assessing AI agents' ability to conduct research, and it is complementary to evaluations on verifiable tasks, as well as blinded reviews of AI outputs. Our results show early evidence that even though agents are proficient on verifiable research tasks, they do not make genuine progress on open-ended ones. It is worth understanding if this is a fundamental limit, or if better models, scaffolds, and more compute could help close it. As the evidence for the gap between open-ended and verifiable tasks firms up, it is also worth understanding how much progress in AI depends on open-ended research rather than hill-climbing on well-specified objectives. In follow-up studies, we are expanding the set of non-public papers we evaluate. If you are an AI researcher with unpublished papers, we would love to collaborate with you on our next shadow evaluation. Expression of interest: forms.gle/CEcA4JmYhDWXQGot8 Conducting shadow evaluations involves a lot of researcher degrees of freedom. In many places, our coauthors disagreed with our interpretation of the findings, and we have surfaced those disagreements in the paper. (This is one reason why having a group of coauthors with different priors is important for open-ended research.) We also release the agent logs, one of the AI-generated papers (the other original paper is still not public), and all the code and data, so that others can conduct their own analyses of our results: cruxevals.com/crux/can-ai-ag… Finally, we plan to conduct shadow evaluations regularly, and are hiring a senior researcher to help lead these efforts. Apply here: cruxevals.com/careers/senior… I'm grateful for the core team leading this effort: @PKirgis , Andrew Schwartz, @steverab , and @random_walker , and to our collaborators who reviewed AI papers, analyzed agents logs, and gave feedback on the paper: @DavidDAfrica , @KozzyVoudouris , Viet Nguyen, Toby Pilditch, @DubMagda , @HarryCoppock , @CUdudec , @nityndg , Matilda Orona, @tilmanbayer , Derrick Chan-Sew, Yue Ling, Abhishek Shetty, @hlntnr , @ghadfield , @sethlazar , @snewmanpv , @shostekofsky , @RishiBommasani

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Yes, LLM architectures are getting a little more complicated

The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

The open-model race is no longer about finding one universally “best” model. Apertus and @allen_ai 's OLMo optimize for transparency. @poolsideai 's Laguna and @Alibaba_Qwen optimize for hardware efficiency. @Macaron0fficial 's Macaron turns one base model into a set of swappable specialists. @Kimi_Moonshot 's K3, @deepseek_ai , @Zai_org 's GLM, and @MiniMax_AI push downloadable capability toward the closed frontier. That changes how you should compare them. > A model can be cheaper to run but harder to load > A model can be fully open but weaker on benchmarks > A model can be downloadable but impractical to host > A model can be modular but add routing failures One leaderboard cannot rank all four approaches well.

The better question is not “which open model is best?” It is “which trade-off fits the task?” We mapped the four camps and built a task-fit matrix for choosing between them. alphasignal.ai/news/the-open… Link The Open-Model Race has Split Four Ways | AlphaSignal Open-weight AI models now optimize for four distinct outcomes—deep transparency, hardware efficiency, modular specialization, or raw frontier capability—making alphasignal.ai

Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over. Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price. We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times. > One switch cost 11x warm > Routing somewhere else cost 47% more > Caches don't transfer between models Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another. The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt. So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%. Which part owns the decision on which model to use?, When will a switch ever become profitable?, And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?

It gets worse because the tax grows with how much context you're carrying. Double the session, and you double the cost of every switch inside it. Cost per 1,000 prefix tokens barely moved across a six-fold change in session size: alphasignal.ai/news/model-ro…

Our breakdown runs the arithmetic they leave out. > 64 instances running at peak > Claude Code caps 16 concurrent > Crossover sits at 17 units > Cheap models cut bills 4x > Two skeptics reviewed every diff They also stubbed broken functions and justified them in comments. processed.summary: Cette journée a été riche en annonces et réflexions dans le monde de l'IA. Les grands acteurs comme OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic et Mistral ont dévoilé de nouveaux modèles et des baisses de prix significatives, rendant l'IA plus accessible et performante. Des débats importants sur la sécurité, l'éthique des modèles ouverts et fermés, ainsi que l'impact de l'IA sur le travail ont animé les discussions, tandis que des conseils pratiques ont émergé pour mieux interagir avec ces systèmes complexes et puissants.

glossaire.definition: Un grand modèle linguistique, c'est un programme d'IA entraîné sur d'énormes quantités de texte pour comprendre, générer et répondre en langage humain.
Les 'tokens' sont les unités de base (mots ou parties de mots) utilisées par les modèles d'IA pour traiter le texte ; le coût et la vitesse d'utilisation de l'IA sont souvent mesurés en tokens.
Des modèles d'IA dont le code et les 'poids' (les paramètres internes appris) sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de les utiliser, de les modifier et de les améliorer.
Des systèmes d'IA capables d'effectuer des tâches complexes de manière autonome, en planifiant des étapes, en utilisant des outils et en interagissant avec leur environnement.
Le processus par lequel un modèle d'IA utilise ce qu'il a appris pour générer une réponse ou faire une prédiction à partir de nouvelles données.
Une technique où un utilisateur malveillant manipule un modèle d'IA pour qu'il ignore ses instructions de sécurité ou qu'il exécute des commandes non autorisées.
Un 'harness' est un cadre ou un environnement logiciel qui permet à un modèle d'IA de se connecter à des outils externes, d'interagir avec des systèmes et d'effectuer des tâches plus complexes.

category_summaries.actu: Plusieurs entreprises majeures de l'IA ont fait des annonces significatives, notamment des baisses de prix importantes pour les modèles GPT-5.6 d'OpenAI, des avancées robotiques avec Gemini Robotics 2 de Google DeepMind, et des partenariats stratégiques pour Mistral AI avec Microsoft. On note aussi des sorties de mode 'furtif' pour des entreprises de matériel IA comme Etched, et des discussions continues sur la transparence et la régulation des modèles d'IA 'de frontière'.
category_summaries.tips: Les développeurs partagent des astuces pour mieux utiliser les LLM, comme l'importance de sessions de 'bavardage' vocal pour aider l'IA à comprendre des tâches complexes, ou l'utilisation de boucles d'agents pour des objectifs ouverts. Il a été souligné comment l'optimisation des 'harness' (environnements d'agents) peut réduire considérablement le coût des interactions avec les modèles. Des conseils pratiques sur la sécurité des 'sandboxes' (environnements isolés pour l'IA) et l'évaluation des agents ont aussi été partagés.
category_summaries.idees: Le débat sur la sécurité et la régulation de l'IA s'intensifie, avec des appels à des tests obligatoires par des tiers et des discussions sur l'importance des modèles open source pour la défense cybernétique. Des réflexions portent sur l'impact de l'IA sur la productivité (l'IA en tant qu'ingénieur junior), la nature de la recherche scientifique menée par l'IA (ses limites en créativité), et les implications économiques (la concentration du pouvoir vs l'accès généralisé). Il est aussi question de la transformation de l'éducation grâce à l'IA personnalisée.

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est de faire de longues sessions de 'bavardage' informel. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste 'divaguer' pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en préambule, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment doués pour reconstruire de longs monologues incohérents et souvent, leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce que vous aviez au départ. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la 'fusion mentale' et avez moins de corrections à faire par la suite.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
highlights.decryptage: Andrej Karpathy explique qu'il est souvent efficace de parler longuement et spontanément à un modèle d'IA (LLM), même de manière désorganisée, car l'IA peut en extraire le sens plus clairement qu'on ne le ferait en tapant, facilitant ainsi la communication.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est de faire de longues sessions de 'bavardage' informel. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste 'divaguer' pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout est permis, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en préambule, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, je le transforme en une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment doués pour reconstruire de longs monologues incohérents et souvent, leur écho de votre propre enchevêtrement de pensées ressort beaucoup plus clair que ce que vous aviez au départ. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la 'fusion mentale' et avez moins de corrections à faire par la suite.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

idees.text_fr: Nouvelle newsletter : LES QUATRE CAVALIERS DE L'APOCALYPSE DE LA BULLE DE L'IA Je ne suis ni anti-IA ni certain que l'IA soit une bulle. Mais les quatre dernières semaines ont montré clairement que le développement de l'IA fait maintenant face à une hydre à quatre têtes très claire. 1. Un risque de dépense, alors que les hyperscalers manquent de liquidités et s'endettent de 170 milliards de dollars par an — ce qui est plus que le déficit projeté du Royaume-Uni. 2. Un risque de revenus, alors que les modèles "open-weight" menacent de comprimer les marges des laboratoires de pointe ... et que l'IA devient le genre d'industrie à forte intensité d'actifs, compétitive au niveau international, nécessitant une cohérence politique stable et déterminée à long terme, ce qui est sans doute l'avantage concurrentiel de la Chine. 3. Un risque politique, alors que le populisme anti-IA devient l'une des lignes d'applaudissement les plus faciles, même si l'IA devient un pilier de plus en plus fondamental de la croissance économique américaine. 4. Un risque technologique, alors que les laboratoires de pointe se concentrent sur la RSI, ce qui, je pense, pourrait modifier considérablement le modèle commercial de base des laboratoires, car les coûts de calcul augmentent pour un ensemble de modèles super-avancés qui sont adaptés et abordables pour une petite minorité d'utilisateurs (par exemple, en cybersécurité). En une phrase : Les capacités de l'IA deviennent plus puissantes, tandis que certains fondements économiques du développement de l'IA — et, comme nous le verrons, le soutien politique à l'IA — deviennent plus vulnérables. L'article d'aujourd'hui (long, 5000 mots) examine en profondeur chaque risque et aussi — parce que la surconfiance dans cet espace est généralement un signe que l'on ne réfléchit pas assez — j'offre la raison la plus solide de penser que chaque risque pourrait être surestimé.
idees.text_original: New newsletter: THE FOUR HORSEMEN OF THE AI BUBBLE APOCALYPSE I am neither anti-AI nor certain that AI is a bubble. But the last four weeks have made clear that the AI buildout now faces a very clear quadruple-headed risk hydra. 1. A spending risk, as the hyperscalers run low on cash and take on $170b in annual debt—which is more than the projected UK deficit. 2. A revenue risk, as open-weight models threaten to compress the margins of frontier labs ... and as AI become the sort of internationally competitive asset-heavy industry requiring stable and determined long-term policy consistency, which is arguably China's competitive advantage. 3. A political risk, as anti-AI populism becomes one of the easiest applause lines, even as AI becomes a more and more foundational pillar of US economic growth 4. A technological risk, as the frontier labs bear down on RSI, which I think could significantly change the basic business model of the labs, as compute costs rise and rise for a set of super-advanced models that are fit for, and affordable to, a small minority of users (in, eg, cyber security) In one sentence: The capabilities of AI are becoming more powerful, while some economic underpinnings of the AI buildout—and, as we’ll discuss, the political support for AI—are becoming more vulnerable. Today's (long, 5k word) piece deeply considers each risk and also—because over-confidence in this space is typically a sign that you're not thinking hard enough—I offer the strongest reason to think each risk might be overblown. derekthompson.org/p/the-four…
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet introduit une réflexion sur les risques majeurs qui pèsent sur le développement de l'IA : les dépenses exorbitantes des entreprises, la concurrence des modèles open source qui réduisent les marges, un potentiel rejet politique de l'IA, et l'augmentation des coûts de calcul pour les modèles les plus avancés, remettant en question la viabilité économique actuelle de la course à l'IA.

idees.text_fr: Il y a quinze ans, @Coursera et les cours en ligne ont changé l'éducation. Cela a mieux fonctionné que presque tout le monde ne l'avait imaginé, en élargissant l'accès en ouvrant les lieux d'apprentissage. Mais la manière d'apprendre reste largement la même depuis des siècles : elle est toujours "taille unique", enseignée de la même manière à chaque personne qui se présente. Nous avons maintenant l'occasion de changer la façon dont l'apprentissage se déroule. Grâce aux avancées de l'IA, nous pouvons maintenant créer un guide d'apprentissage personnalisé pour chaque personne. Nous transformerons l'apprentissage d'un modèle "un-vers-plusieurs" en un modèle "un-vers-un". Je lance LearnVector pour inventer cette prochaine génération d'apprentissage. Nous commençons avec un investissement de 100 millions de dollars de Coursera, et prévoyons de collaborer étroitement avec Coursera et Udemy.
idees.text_original: Fifteen years ago, @Coursera and online courses changed education. It worked better than almost anyone expected, expanding access by opening up where you can learn. But how you learn remains largely the same as it has for centuries: it is still one-size-fits-all, taught the same way to each person who shows up. We now have an opportunity to change how learning happens. With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one‑to‑many to one‑to‑one. I'm starting LearnVector to invent this next generation of learning. We are starting with a $100M investment from Coursera, and plan to collaborate closely with Coursera and Udemy. Good learning needs much more than just a chatbot. Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you. In contrast, LearnVector will plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you’ve mastered new skills. One thing has not changed in all this time. People want learning they can trust: material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it. Anything less wastes the most valuable thing a learner has: time. Coursera has a trusted library of materials from authoritative sources. LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to bring this trustworthy learning to everyone. I'm grateful to Greg Hart and the entire Coursera team for supporting LearnVector. I look forward to working with our talented team to change how we learn, and accelerate human development. learnvector.ai
idees.decryptage: Andrew Ng, une figure majeure de l'IA, lance "LearnVector" avec un gros investissement pour révolutionner l'éducation en utilisant l'IA. L'objectif est de passer d'un enseignement "pour tous" à un apprentissage "un-à-un" entièrement personnalisé pour chaque élève, contrairement aux simples chatbots qui peuvent nuire à l'apprentissage s'ils sont mal utilisés.

Il critique l'idée que les modèles fermés sont plus sûrs comme étant une tentative de contrôle du marché.

idees.text_fr: Adam Thierer avait écrit le livre marquant sur "l'innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas à demander la permission au gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. La protection de l'IA open source est maintenant un élément essentiel pour garantir cela.
idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m
idees.decryptage: Andrew Ng met en garde contre l'idée de demander la permission au gouvernement pour innover dans l'IA, en défendant l'IA open source comme un moteur essentiel de l'innovation et de la liberté, et en craignant que sa restriction n'étouffe le progrès.

idees.text_original: This is a good piece, and, as I responded last time @DKThomp wrote about a potential bubble in the fall - I don't know the future, but a financial bubble (if there is one) is not a bubble around AI ability For better or worse, AI is not going to go away (or even stop developing) Derek Thompson (@DKThomp) New newsletter: THE FOUR HORSEMEN OF THE AI BUBBLE APOCALYPSE I am neither anti-AI nor certain that AI is a bubble. But the last four weeks have made clear that the AI buildout now faces a very clear quadruple-headed risk hydra. 1. A spending risk, as the hyperscalers run low on cash and take on $170b in annual debt—which is more than the projected UK deficit. 2. A revenue risk, as open-weight models threaten to compress the margins of frontier labs ... and as AI become the sort of internationally competitive asset-heavy industry requiring stable and determined long-term policy consistency, which is arguably China's competitive advantage. 3. A political risk, as anti-AI populism becomes one of the easiest applause lines, even as AI becomes a more and more foundational pillar of US economic growth 4. A technological risk, as the frontier labs bear down on RSI, which I think could significantly change the basic business model of the labs, as compute costs rise and rise for a set of super-advanced models that are fit for, and affordable to, a small minority of users (in, eg, cyber security) In one sentence: The capabilities of AI are becoming more powerful, while some economic underpinnings of the AI buildout—and, as we’ll discuss, the political support for AI—are becoming more vulnerable. Today's (long, 5k word) piece deeply considers each risk and also—because over-confidence in this space is typically a sign that you're not thinking hard enough—I offer the strongest reason to think each risk might be overblown. derekthompson.org/p/the-four… — https://nitter.net/DKThomp/status/2083174287897207220#m

idees.text_fr: Mark Zuckerberg a raison : « La question fondamentale de notre époque n'est pas de savoir si la superintelligence existera, mais qui y aura accès. Sera-t-elle centralisée et limitée à quelques institutions, ou sera-t-elle un outil qui donnera du pouvoir à tout le monde ? » La concentration du pouvoir est le plus grand risque de l'IA. Quand un petit nombre de laboratoires (travaillant main dans la main avec l'État) décident qui a accès à quelles capacités de modèle, ils façonnent inévitablement ce qui peut être dit, connu et construit. Ce n'est pas de la "sécurité". C'est du contrôle. Comme le souligne Mark, l'histoire de l'open source montre qu'un large accès et une transparence sont généralement le meilleur chemin vers une sécurité et une résilience réelles. La décentralisation crée des contre-pouvoirs. En revanche, les alternatives centralisées, comme les régimes d'approbation bureaucratiques et le "gatekeeping" obligatoire, produisent généralement une capture réglementaire et renforcent les cartels. Une superintelligence personnelle entre les mains de tous, avec des modèles concurrents et une réelle souveraineté des données, est un bien meilleur rempart contre un avenir dystopique que des gardiens autoproclamés qui se disent "alignés" avec toute l'humanité.
idees.text_original: Mark Zuckerberg gets it right: “The defining question of our age isn’t whether superintelligence will exist, but who will have access to it. Will it be centralized and restricted to a few institutions, or will it be a tool that empowers everyone?” Concentration of power is the biggest risk of AI. When a small number of labs (working hand-in-glove with the administrative state) decide who has access to which model capabilities, they inevitably shape what can be said, known, and built. That’s not “safety.” It’s control. As Mark points out, the history of open source shows that broad access and transparency are usually the best path to actual security and resilience. Decentralization creates checks and balances on power. By contrast, centralized alternatives, like bureaucratic approval regimes and mandatory gatekeeping, typically produce regulatory capture and reinforce cartels. Personal superintelligence in everyone’s hands, with competing models and real data sovereignty, is a far better check on a dystopian future than self-appointed guardians who claim to be “aligned” with all of humanity. Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) I wrote about why we believe the future is for everyone. More coming about a positive vision for a world with superintelligence soon. — https://nitter.net/finkd/status/2082160210399948869#m

idees.text_fr: La course aux modèles ouverts ne consiste plus à trouver un modèle universellement "meilleur". Apertus et OLMo de @allen_ai optimisent la transparence. Laguna de @poolsideai et Qwen de @Alibaba_Qwen optimisent l'efficacité matérielle. Macaron de @Macaron0fficial transforme un modèle de base en un ensemble de spécialistes interchangeables. K3 de @Kimi_Moonshot, @deepseek_ai, GLM de @Zai_org, et @MiniMax_AI poussent la capacité téléchargeable vers la frontière "fermée". Cela change la façon de les comparer. > Un modèle peut être moins cher à exécuter mais plus difficile à charger > Un modèle peut être entièrement ouvert mais moins performant sur les "benchmarks" > Un modèle peut être téléchargeable mais peu pratique à héberger > Un modèle peut être modulaire mais ajouter des échecs de routage. Un seul "leaderboard" ne peut pas bien classer ces quatre approches.
idees.text_original: The open-model race is no longer about finding one universally “best” model. Apertus and @allen_ai 's OLMo optimize for transparency. @poolsideai 's Laguna and @Alibaba_Qwen optimize for hardware efficiency. @Macaron0fficial 's Macaron turns one base model into a set of swappable specialists. @Kimi_Moonshot 's K3, @deepseek_ai , @Zai_org 's GLM, and @MiniMax_AI push downloadable capability toward the closed frontier. That changes how you should compare them. > A model can be cheaper to run but harder to load > A model can be fully open but weaker on benchmarks > A model can be downloadable but impractical to host > A model can be modular but add routing failures One leaderboard cannot rank all four approaches well.
idees.decryptage: Le tweet explique qu'il n'y a plus un seul "meilleur" modèle d'IA open source, car ils sont optimisés pour des objectifs différents (transparence, efficacité matérielle, spécialisation, capacité brute), rendant leur comparaison complexe et dépendante de l'utilisation spécifique.

idees.text_fr: La meilleure question n'est pas "quel modèle ouvert est le meilleur ?" C'est "quel compromis convient à la tâche ?" Nous avons cartographié les quatre camps et construit une matrice d'adéquation aux tâches pour choisir entre eux.
idees.text_original: The better question is not “which open model is best?” It is “which trade-off fits the task?” We mapped the four camps and built a task-fit matrix for choosing between them. alphasignal.ai/news/the-open… Link The Open-Model Race has Split Four Ways | AlphaSignal Open-weight AI models now optimize for four distinct outcomes—deep transparency, hardware efficiency, modular specialization, or raw frontier capability—making alphasignal.ai
idees.decryptage: Plutôt que de chercher le modèle d'IA "ouvert" le plus performant, il est plus pertinent de se demander quel modèle est le mieux adapté à une tâche spécifique, en fonction de ses compromis (coût, performance, facilité d'utilisation, transparence).

idees.text_fr: Votre routeur de modèles vous facture onze fois le contexte que vous avez déjà payé. Les caches de prompt appartiennent à un seul modèle. Si vous changez de modèle pendant une session, le nouveau modèle relira tout depuis le début, au prix fort. Nous l'avons évalué avec trois tailles de session différentes. Les mêmes 12 tours, exécutés cinq fois. > Un changement a coûté 11 fois plus cher > Le routage vers un autre endroit a coûté 47 % de plus > Les caches ne sont pas transférées entre les modèles. Grok 4.5 donne un résultat cinq fois moins cher que le modèle qu'il a remplacé. Le changement de prix était de 0,2 % dans un test, et de 7,9 % dans un autre. Le deuxième problème est caché sous tout cela. Claude compte 58 % de tokens de plus que GPT pour le même prompt. Donc, dépenser 2 $ au lieu de 5 $ n'est pas une économie de 60 %. Sur le même prompt, c'est plus proche de 37 %. Quelle partie possède la décision sur le modèle à utiliser ?, Quand un changement deviendra-t-il rentable ?, Et pourquoi cela devient-il encore plus cher avec des exécutions plus longues ?
idees.text_original: Your model router charges you for context that you've already paid for, eleven times over. Prompt caches belong to one model. Change the model during a session, and the new model will read everything all over again, at the full price. We priced it with three different session sizes. Same 12 turns, run five times. > One switch cost 11x warm > Routing somewhere else cost 47% more > Caches don't transfer between models Grok 4.5 gives output five times cheaper than the model it took over from. Price change was 0.2% in one test, and 7.9% in another. The second issue is hidden under all of that. Claude counts 58% more tokens than GPT for the same prompt. So, spending $2 instead of $5 is not a 60% savings. On the same prompt, it's closer to 37%. Which part owns the decision on which model to use?, When will a switch ever become profitable?, And why does it become even more expensive with longer runs?

outils.text_fr: Excités d'annoncer les Projets, qui sont les centres de Perplexity pour la collaboration agent-humain. La plupart de mon temps se passe maintenant dans les Projets, où les agents gèrent automatiquement leurs propres fichiers persistants et collaborent avec des outils natifs. Les Projets sont le cœur de la collaboration de Perplexity : à mesure que les agents deviennent plus durables, ils auront besoin de moyens plus natifs pour persister et s'améliorer : mémoires, compétences et fichiers. Mais jusqu'à aujourd'hui, les agents n'avaient pas de centre de collaboration central permettant une zone persistante pour le travail intellectuel. Cet endroit, ce sont les Projets, et non les chats ou les fichiers individuels. Les Projets sont livrés avec un ensemble d'outils CLI conçus intentionnellement pour que les agents collaborent entre fichiers, projets et avec d'autres agents. Surtout, les identités individuelles et de projet sont entièrement fonctionnelles. Les connecteurs individuels sont pris en charge comme d'habitude, mais aussi les identifiants au niveau du projet. Un agent cérébral au niveau du projet gère le projet et fournit des résumés objectifs et des mémoires. Les agents effectuent l'exécution, mais les humains continuent de diriger avec des notifications et des vérifications de permissions. En interne chez Perplexity, la manière canonique de travailler est maintenant de commencer dans Slack (chaque Projet se connecte à au moins un canal Slack), de générer plusieurs fils de conversation en parallèle, d'accepter la plupart des premières passes, et de suivre dans les applications de Perplexity lorsque des raffinements sont nécessaires. L'avenir du travail intellectuel s'annonce radieux : le travail est incroyablement efficace avec des outils comme Computer, laissant plus de temps à la curiosité et à l'apprentissage. Les Projets sont la prochaine étape de la vision que les Espaces ont initiée pour la collaboration et le stockage persistant du contexte. Nous sommes impatients de voir comment vous utiliserez les Projets et nous apprendrons de vos retours pour continuer à repousser les limites de ce qui est possible lorsque les agents et les humains travaillent ensemble pour construire de vraies entreprises.
outils.text_original: Excited to announce Projects, which are Perplexity's hubs for agent and human collaboration. Most of my time now lives in Projects, where agents automatically manage their own persistent files and collaborate with native tools. Projects are Perplexity's core for collaboration: as agents become more long-running, they will need more agent-native ways to persist and self-improve: memories, skills, and files. But until today, agents have lacked a central hub for collaboration that allows for a persistent area for knowledge work. That place is Projects, not individual chats or files. Projects come packaged with an set of CLI tools intentionally designed for agents to collaborate across files, projects, and with other agents. A project-level brain agent manages the project and provides objective summaries and memories. Agents do the execution but humans still do the steering with notifications and permissions checks. The future of knowledge work is looking bright: work is incredibly efficient with tools like Computer, leaving more time for curiosity and learning. Projects is the next step in the vision that Spaces began for collaboration and persistent storage of context. We're excited to see how you use Projects and we will learn from your feedback to keep pushing the frontier of what is possible when agents and humans work together to build real businesses. outils.text_fr: Nouveau cours : Créez des applications LLM qui répondent rapidement aux requêtes des utilisateurs en fonctionnant sur du matériel conçu pour une inférence rapide. Ce court cours a été conçu avec @Cerebras et enseigné par @zhennydez, @duerr_seb et @MilksandMatcha. Lorsqu'un modèle génère du texte, une grande partie du temps est consacrée au déplacement de ses "poids" de la mémoire vers les unités de calcul. Le matériel optimisé pour l'inférence minimise ce mouvement, rendant la génération de tokens plusieurs fois plus rapide que sur une configuration GPU typique. Dans ce cours, le matériel que vous utiliserez est le "Wafer-Scale Engine" de Cerebras, qui est conçu pour une inférence rapide en maintenant les "poids" du modèle près des unités de calcul. Une inférence rapide accélère les workflows d'agents longs et débloque également des applications en temps réel sensibles à la latence comme la traduction en direct et les agents vocaux.
outils.text_original: New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. outils.text_fr: La figure de l'architecture Kimi K3 pour la grande sortie du modèle "open-weight" d'hier, avec quelques observations et réflexions. 1. Oui, cela semble relativement compliqué, mais c'est essentiellement une version de production "scalée" de leur modèle Kimi Linear sorti l'année dernière (passé de 48B à 2.8T ; K3 est de loin le plus grand modèle "open-weight" à l'heure actuelle). 2. Le seul nouveau composant par rapport à Kimi Linear est le LatentMoE. Je l'ai omis dans la figure ci-dessous car elle est déjà très chargée, mais c'est essentiellement le même LatentMoE que dans Nemotron 3 Ultra. L'idée ici est de compresser (projeter vers le bas) de grandes couches linéaires, de manière similaire à l'attention latente multi-têtes. 3. La tendance générale de Kimi K3 (similaire à Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4 et d'autres) est également vers une meilleure efficacité d'inférence. C'est-à-dire qu'il y a de nombreux composants qui remplacent les composants existants par des versions optimisées pour l'efficacité. Par exemple, MoE -> LatentMoE, attention régulière -> attention latente multi-têtes et Kimi Delta Attention. 4. Le seul changement de composant qui n'est pas une optimisation d'efficacité est les résiduels d'attention. Comme DeepSeek V4 a amélioré le chemin résiduel avec mHC (Hyper-Connexions contraintes par la variété), les résiduels d'attention sont un moyen d'améliorer le chemin résiduel, mais cela fonctionne un peu différemment. Selon le rapport, cela améliore la perte de validation et les performances en aval (un peu) de manière constante et ajoute environ 4 % au coût d'entraînement et 2 % au coût d'inférence. 5. Fait intéressant, Kimi K3 s'est débarrassé de toutes les couches RoPE et utilise NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) partout à la place. Dans d'autres architectures, la tendance récente était plutôt vers RoPE dans les couches d'attention locales (comme l'attention à fenêtre glissante) et NoPE dans les couches globales. Il y avait quelques architectures qui n'utilisaient que NoPE partout, mais c'est la première de niveau "frontière" à ma connaissance. 6. Kimi K3 a maintenant également un support multimodal natif, ce qui est génial ! Il y a plusieurs autres détails d'entraînement intéressants dans le rapport technique, mais c'est tout pour le front architectural jusqu'à présent. Une très belle sortie dans l'ensemble.
outils.text_original: The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

outils.text_fr: Mistral OCR 4 a transformé un examen de calcul manuscrit en LaTeX propre ! Nous lui avons donné une photo d'une page d'examen manuscrite. Le modèle a lu l'écriture et reconstruit chaque formule en texte numérique structuré. Mais c'est la partie révélatrice : la plupart des outils OCR se contentent de "dumper" le texte et de laisser la figure de côté. OCR 4 a détecté le tracé, l'a encadré et l'a étiqueté comme un graphique. Il n'est pas redessiné, mais il est lu et pris en compte.

The graph, unfortunately, it didn’t redraw. But that’s the telling part: most OCR tools just dump the text and quietly drop the figure. OCR 4 caught the plot, boxed it, and tagged it as a chart. It doesn’t get redrawn, but it gets read and accounted for Video Mistral AI (@MistralAI) Introducing Mistral OCR 4.
